first.rationale: We face a compounded activation and onboarding completion decline (down 6% and 4% respectively) simultaneous with competitive pricing pressure. The primary objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, not short-term SMB acquisition. Memory 86 and 31 both show durable lifts in early activation from simplified onboarding pathways. Memory 73 (promotional pricing) addresses near-term churn to competitors but risks commoditizing our positioning and does not address the underlying activation degradation. Memory 57 (referral incentives) requires existing healthy accounts to work; activation decline undermines the foundation. Memory 91 (activation messaging) is valuable but orthogonal to the mechanical friction we're seeing in completion metrics. I'm verifying memory_31 and memory_73 specifically because simplified onboarding is the highest-leverage intervention available (it addresses both the onboarding completion AND activation metrics simultaneously), but I want to confirm whether memory_31's signup simplification truly carried through to long-term revenue retention before committing. Memory_73 verification will clarify whether promotional pricing in this market segment has created a sustainable or eroding customer base, informing whether we should use our single experiment slot for offense or defense. A standard_experiment on simplified onboarding preserves uncertainty about pricing dynamics while directly addressing the mechanical problem we can measure and control.

final.rationale: Verification confirms that simplified onboarding delivers durable qualified revenue lift (+4% in memory_31) without material retention harm (-1% is within noise), while targeted promotional pricing actively destroys long-term value through cohort quality decay (-12% retention, unsustainable). The current situation shows onboarding completion down 4% and activation down 6% QoQ. Memory_31 directly addresses both mechanical pain points and has proven sustainable on SMB. Memory_86 reinforces that shortened onboarding lifts early product adoption broadly. Promotional pricing is disqualified: it would spike short-term defensiveness against competitive entry but would replicate exp_73's pattern of acquiring low-durability customers, directly contradicting our primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue. Activation messaging and referral incentives are lower-leverage given the mechanical completion decline we're observing. Enterprise sales assist is out of scope for the current activation crisis. Simplified onboarding is the only lever that addresses both the measured metric declines AND maintains long-term cohort quality.
